idiom_name: begin()/end() iterator type consumed by range-based for (C++11)
implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization is a small type that models the iterator protocol - begin()/end(), operator++, operator*, operator!= - so the range-based for loop and the standard algorithms drive it; keep the production state inside the iterator and the end value cheap. Since C++20 the same sequence can be written as a coroutine generator (co_yield) and C++23 adds std::generator to the standard library, which the capability floor promotes when the toolchain is C++20 or newer; ranges::views are the declarative alternative when the sequence is a lazy transformation of an existing range rather than a stateful producer.
pitfalls: Iterators are copied freely (range-based for copies begin()): a producer whose state is not fully captured in the iterator object - a shared buffer, a file handle, an implicit this pointer - duplicates or dangles on the second copy, so make copies independent or delete the copy constructor.
Generator types that yield references into an internal buffer are invalidated by the next increment (the classic iterator-invalidation rule); return by value unless profiling justifies the reference.

begin()/end() semantics must be decided: equality-comparable end iterators work for finite sequences, but stateful producers usually need a sentinel-type end (std::default_sentinel_t, C++20) or an explicit exhausted state, and mixing the two silently produces endless loops.

variants.name: C++20 coroutine generator (co_yield; std::generator in C++23)
variants.idiom_name: co_yield in a coroutine returning std::generator<T> (C++23) or a custom generator type (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: A generator coroutine writes the sequence as straight-line code: the return type carries a promise type (initial_suspend, yield_value, final_suspend), the body calls co_yield per element, and a range-based for loop drives it; C++20 supplies co_yield, and C++23 adds std::generator, which removes the hand-written promise type and gives the standard shape. The coroutine frame owns the state, so destroying the generator runs the frame's destructors - RAII cleanup for free - which is why this variant wins wherever the toolchain allows it.
pitfalls: Coroutine frames allocate: per-element generators in hot loops pay a heap allocation unless the compiler applies heap-allocation elision (HALO), which it is not required to do.
The frame keeps references, not referents: resuming a generator after the object it points to has died is undefined behaviour, and a std::generator must not outlive the range it borrows.

Once a std::generator is exhausted it compares equal to std::default_sentinel, and incrementing past exhaustion is undefined behaviour - loops must test the sentinel instead of assuming a repeatable end state.
